spans.text: The only conscious and serious attempt at the documentation and analysis of an Eskimo Pidgin is the article by Vilhjálmur Stefánsson (1909) on the so-called Eskimo Trade Jargon of Herschel Island, which is based mainly on North Alaskan Iñupiaq, Siglitun (the Mackenzie dialect of Western Canadian Inuktun), and English, but which also contains words of Athabaskan, Hawaiian, Portuguese, and Scandinavian origin, some of which may have come via other pidgins.

spans.text: These pidgins were also used by Westerners in the fur trade, and it may be difficult both to determine whether they already existed before contact with Westerners and to distinguish them from the Eskimo Pidgins that originated in contact with Westerners.

The only conscious and serious attempt at the documentation and analysis of an Eskimo Pidgin is the article by Vilhjálmur Stefánsson (1909) on the so-called Eskimo Trade Jargon of Herschel Island, which is based mainly on North Alaskan Iñupiaq, Siglitun (the Mackenzie dialect of Western Canadian Inuktun), and English, but which also contains words of Athabaskan, Hawaiian, Portuguese, and Scandinavian origin, some of which may have come via other pidgins.
In addition to these mainly seasonal contacts, there were permanent contacts between Inuit and Westerners in which Eskimo Pidgins were used.
Furthermore in the 19th century, Scots and Americans organized whaling expeditions in the Hudson Bay, while Russians traded in the Bering Strait.
